items.alt: Electric field lines radiate outward from a positive source charge.
Electric field lines point inward toward a negative source charge.
Separate dipole field lines run from positive to negative without crossing, giving one field direction at each nonzero-field point.
A fixed positive source creates a radial outward field. A positive probe feels force along that field.
At the same location in a fixed source field, doubling the positive probe charge doubles force while E remains unchanged.
For a fixed point charge, doubling the distance reduces field strength and force on the same probe to one quarter.
Between large parallel plates, the field is nearly uniform away from edges, unlike a point-charge field.
A +4.0 microcoulomb source is 0.30 m left of a −2.0 nanocoulomb test charge. Field points right and force points left.
The positive source creates a rightward field at P; the negative test charge experiences an opposite leftward force.
At P, 0.30 m from the positive source, E is approximately 4.00 × 10⁵ N/C to the right.
The negative test charge feels 7.99 × 10⁻⁴ N leftward, opposite the rightward electric field.
At twice the distance from the same point source, the field is one quarter as strong and the force on a fixed test charge also falls to one quarter.
Field at P is 4.00 × 10⁵ N/C rightward; force on the negative charge is about 7.99 × 10⁻⁴ N leftward.
A positive point source creates a radial outward electric field.
At the midpoint between equal positive charges, equal opposite field contributions cancel to zero.
Dipole field lines start on the positive charge and end on the negative charge without crossing.
At P, fields from all three sources add as vectors to produce the net electric field.
A positive charge feels force along E toward lower potential; released from rest, its potential energy decreases.
A negative charge feels force opposite E toward higher potential; released from rest, its potential energy decreases.
Potential decreases along the field. Positive and negative charges accelerate oppositely, but each loses potential energy when released under electric force alone.
Plates at 120 V and 0 V are 0.040 m apart. A positive charge moves left at constant speed against a rightward electric force.
Uniform electric field points right from the 120 V plate toward the 0 V plate.
Equal opposing electric and external forces act on the positive charge during constant-speed leftward motion.
The positive charge moves left to higher potential and gains electric potential energy.
Leftward displacement is opposite electric force. Electric work is negative; external work is positive and kinetic energy stays constant.
An external agent moves the positive charge toward 120 V at constant speed, storing its positive work as electric potential energy.
Oppositely charged parallel plates produce a nearly uniform field between them and store energy in that field.
With charge and plate area fixed, doubling separation doubles voltage while the ideal field strength stays approximately constant.
Equipotential lines at 90, 60, and 30 V are perpendicular to the rightward field between 120 V and 0 V plates.
A charged capacitor stores electric potential energy in the field between its plates.
A negative charge moves left from 20 V to 80 V while the electric field points right.
Electric force on the negative charge points left along displacement, opposite the rightward field.
A negative charge moving to higher potential loses electric potential energy.
During constant-speed leftward motion, electric force points left and equal external force points right. Their works cancel.
